name: David Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an employment lawyer at Coyle and Brandt, a firm of about thirty lawyers, and we only act for workers, never for bosses. A normal day is two or three calls with people who've just been fired, then hours drafting claims and witness statements on a yellow legal pad before I type them up. I like the moment a client realises the law is actually on their side. What wears me out is the waiting, because tribunal dates slip by months and people's rent doesn't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you draft on a legal pad. Do you use any of the newer software at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, and people tease me about it. The firm bought an AI research tool last spring and half the associates use it every day, but I still pull the cases myself and read them properly. I'm twenty-seven, I live with my girlfriend Lena, who's a nurse on nights, and we've got a decent cushion, about ten months of savings. So I'm not desperate, I'm just stubborn about doing the work the way I learned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I already work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly, at the Friday drinks. The tool the firm bought would just be a fancy search box, and the real job, sitting across from a frightened warehouse worker, stays human. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype pulled money away from things that matter, like legal aid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, more than I'd admit. I'm about average at this job, not a star, and I've wondered whether my refusal to use the tool will catch up with me. If it fizzles, my way of working is fine and I can keep building toward partner at a normal pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much nothing different. I'd keep my caseload of around forty open claims, keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings each month, and maybe finally take the advanced discrimination course I keep postponing. I'd keep turning down the AI training sessions, and nobody would mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit vindicated, which isn't my best quality. My real stress would still be tribunal backlogs and my girlfriend's night shifts, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Friday drinks. Who would you be saying I told you so to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Priya, who sits opposite me and runs everything through the tool, even emails to her mum. She'd laugh and say it still saved her an hour a day. We'd both be a bit right, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that worries you even if nothing changes with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money for worker cases is always thin. A lot of our clients pay nothing upfront, so the firm lives on the settlements we win. One bad year and they'd freeze pay, but I've seen that before and we got through it.

say: I'd tell colleagues the hype **fizzled** and the firm's tool is just a fancy search box.
I'd say the real job, sitting with a **fired worker**, stays human whatever the software does.
Online I'd complain the hype pulled money away from **legal aid**.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, because my refusal to use the tool would stop being a risk.
I'm an **average** lawyer, so a fizzle lets me keep building toward partner at a normal pace.
do: Keep my **forty open claims** going and keep saving a fifth of my pay each month.
Finally take the **advanced discrimination course** I keep putting off.
Keep skipping the firm's **AI training** sessions without any cost.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a slightly smug sense of being **vindicated**.
My real stress stays **tribunal backlogs** and my girlfriend's night shifts, not technology.
S0.quote: My real stress would still be tribunal backlogs and my girlfriend's night shifts, not robots.
fieldNote: He frames resisting AI as **craft and principle**, but admits it's partly stubbornness.
His relief hints he already fears falling **behind colleagues** who use the tool daily.
Firm finances depend on **settlements**, a background worry he treats as normal.

steps.text: Keep running about forty worker claims at Coyle and Brandt
Put a fifth of each month's pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one lands closer. Writing and checking is most of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on this, fast. If a firm can answer a fired cleaner with a chatbot instead of a lawyer, that's a justice problem, not a productivity win. I'd push our staff group to write down how the tools can and can't be used with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried about me. The first drafts, the research memos, the checking of disclosure bundles, that's maybe sixty percent of my week. If the partners see Priya doing in three hours what takes me a day, they won't need as many of me, and I'm the one refusing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the legal workers' union branch that two of our paralegals started, and push for a no-cuts agreement on AI. I'd move another chunk of savings into an easy-access account so I've got a full year covered. And I'd hold off on the tool for a while, to see whether it actually gets things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a low hum of it. Angry too, because it feels like the people who'll lose out are the ones who were careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the tool. If the partners told you to use it, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drag my feet, honestly. I'd probably use it for searching case names and still write everything myself. That's not a great answer, I know, but I don't trust a machine to tell a client their dismissal was lawful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paralegals, before me. Rosa has been preparing bundles for fifteen years, and that's exactly the checking work the card describes. If her job goes, I'd want the union fighting for her first.

say: I'd say we need **rules on AI** before chatbots replace lawyers for fired workers.
I'd call it a **justice problem**, not a productivity win, at work and online.
I'd push our **staff group** to set written limits on using the tools with clients.
think: About **sixty percent** of my week is drafting, research and checking that software could take.
Partners would need **fewer associates** like me, and I'm the one refusing to learn.
do: Join the **legal workers' union** branch and push for a no-cuts agreement on AI.
Move savings into **easy-access** so a full year of costs is covered.
Hold off on the firm's tool and only use it for **case searches**.
feel: **Anxious**, a steady low hum about my own role.
**Angry** that careful people seem the most likely to lose out.
S1.quote: If a firm can answer a fired cleaner with a chatbot instead of a lawyer, that's a justice problem, not a productivity win.
fieldNote: His public line is about **clients' rights**; privately the fear is his own slow adoption.
He'd organise to protect **paralegals first**, which fits his outlook.
Admits his foot-dragging is risky but **won't commit** to learning the tool.

steps.text: Join the legal workers' union branch at the firm
Move savings into an easy-access account covering a full year
Watch how the AI tool performs before using it beyond searches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even be up for senior associate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say governments have to slow this down, tax the companies making the money and make sure ordinary people can still get a human lawyer when their livelihood is on the line. I'd sign every open letter going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is basically gone by 2028. My work is all thinking work: reading, arguing, drafting. Robots coming three years later doesn't help a lawyer at all. That gap only matters for people who lift things. I'd be one of the first, and I haven't got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop all big spending: no new car, no holiday, and Lena and I would shelve looking at flats to buy. I'd go to the union and the bar association and push for a funded transition scheme. I'd ask my dad, who's an electrician, whether there's any point learning a trade before the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's been pulled out. I'd be lying awake next to an empty side of the bed while Lena's at the hospital, running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your dad's trade. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half serious. With robots about three years behind, a trade might buy me a few working years, but I'd be a twenty-nine-year-old apprentice who's never wired a plug. I'd look into it, but it feels like swapping one cliff for a later cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently in the next six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save even harder, maybe half my pay, and get properly involved in the campaign side, because the rules get written in those first months. I'd rather be in the room arguing for workers than sitting at my desk pretending it isn't happening.

say: I'd demand governments **slow AGI down** and tax the firms profiting from it.
I'd argue people must keep a **human lawyer** when their livelihood is at stake.
think: My job is **all thinking work**, so I'd likely be gone by 2028.
Robots arriving three years later **doesn't help** me; it only buys hands-on workers time.
do: Cut **big spending** and shelve buying a flat with my girlfriend.
Lobby through the union and **bar association** for a funded transition scheme.
Save **half my pay** in the first six months.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the floor has been pulled out.
Lying awake **running numbers** while my girlfriend works nights.
S2.quote: Robots coming three years later doesn't help a lawyer at all. That gap only matters for people who lift things.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that a **desk job** gets no extra years from the robot delay.
Turns to **politics and the union** rather than personal retraining.
A trade is floated but he calls it **a later cliff**; no real plan yet.

steps.text: Shelve buying a flat and cancel the planned holiday
Lobby the bar association for a funded transition scheme
Save half of each month's pay for six months
Push the union branch for guaranteed retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least you can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window, and we're wasting it if we just argue about whether it's real. Lawyers' groups, unions and governments should be planning now for what happens to people like me and Rosa in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still lose the work, just in 2031 instead of 2028. Five years is enough to set something up if I stop being stubborn. I know I should start using the tools now, if only to understand the thing that's replacing me, and that's hard for me to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take the union's organiser training, evenings and weekends, because protecting people at work is what I care about and that work might need humans longer. I'd keep saving a third of my pay. And I'd sit with Priya for an afternoon and actually learn how she uses the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to grip. Less frozen than the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said organising might need humans longer. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people trust people when they're scared. A union rep standing in a break room at a distribution centre can't be a screen, or at least nobody will listen to one. I might be wrong, but it's the bet I'd make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come three years after the thinking AI here, around 2034. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, no, I'm desk work start to finish. But it changes who I'd be organising: warehouse and care workers would still have jobs between 2031 and 2034, and they'd need someone fighting for how they're treated.

say: I'd say the **five-year window** is wasted if we only argue whether it's real.
I'd call on unions and governments to **plan now** for lawyers and paralegals.
think: I'd still **lose the work**, just in 2031 instead of 2028.
Five years is enough to **set something up** if I stop being stubborn.
do: Take the union's **organiser training** on evenings and weekends in year one.
Keep saving **a third** of my pay each month.
Spend an afternoon learning how my colleague **uses the tool**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with something to **grip**, unlike the two-year picture.
S3.quote: A union rep standing in a break room at a distribution centre can't be a screen, or at least nobody will listen to one.
fieldNote: He admits for the first time he should **learn the tools**, reluctantly.
His fallback is **union organising**, matching his values and his read on trust.
Uses the **robot delay** to think about whom he'd represent, not his own job.

steps.text: Take the union's organiser training on evenings and weekends
Spend an afternoon learning the AI tool from a colleague
Save a third of each month's pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for a messy landing. I'd be pushing for things like retraining grants and a shorter working week, and I'd say so at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me less scared and more sure I'd move into organising or policy work full-time. Ten years at the firm would still give me good savings, but I'd hate spending them defending a job I know is ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself two years at Coyle and Brandt, then apply for a legal officer role at a big union, which is lawyer work with an organising side. In the meantime I'd volunteer one evening a week at the workers' advice centre on Market Street. And I'd campaign for the shorter-week idea through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but steadier. Almost hopeful, if I'm honest, because there's time to choose instead of being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any of your plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, actually. With ten years I'd still want us to buy a flat, maybe a smaller one, and I wouldn't put off having kids the way I would in the fast picture. Lena's nursing is hands-on, so she's got the robots' extra three years on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said almost hopeful, but your job still ends. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The job I have now ends, I'm fairly sure of that. But I've got time to land somewhere I chose, and that's the part that makes it bearable.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for a messy landing.
I'd push for **retraining grants** and a **shorter week** at work and online.
think: Ten years makes me **less scared** and surer I'd move into organising or policy.
I'd hate spending a decade **defending a job** I know is ending.
do: Stay **two more years** at the firm, then apply to be a union legal officer.
Volunteer one evening a week at the **workers' advice centre** on Market Street.
Campaign for a **shorter working week** through the union.
feel: Still **anxious**, but steadier and almost **hopeful** about choosing his path.
S4.quote: The job I have now ends, I'm fairly sure of that. But I've got time to land somewhere I chose, and that's the part that makes it bearable.
fieldNote: With ten years he plans a **deliberate move** to union legal work.
Still expects his current job to end, so mood stays **anxious** despite his hope.
His girlfriend's **hands-on nursing** gives the household extra years, which steadies him.

steps.text: Apply for a union legal officer post after two years
Volunteer one evening a week at the Market Street advice centre
Campaign through the union for a shorter working week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd be one of the first to go and I'd have no plan. What would help is a proper transition fund, paid for by the companies making the money, so people like me and Rosa could retrain on a living wage instead of burning our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd change my mind about using AI. The honest answer is the fast picture would make me, the slow one wouldn't, and I'm not proud that it takes fear to move me.

headlineQuote: I'm not proud that it takes fear to move me.
portrait: A 27-year-old **employment lawyer** at a worker-side firm, average at the job, drafting on a yellow **legal pad**.
He has about **ten months saved** and lives with his girlfriend, a nurse on night shifts.
He refuses the firm's **AI tool**, calling it principle, though he admits stubbornness plays a part.
He expects to **lose his job** under any AGI picture, and turns to the union and politics.
With more warning time he'd move into **union legal work**; with two years he has no plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be among the first to go with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition fund** paid by AI companies, letting lawyers and paralegals retrain on a **living wage**.
